title: What We Owe Every Student, Every Day
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek, a former teacher, technology director and policymaker, explains why he wrote The School Leader's Guide to Digital Wellness and how schools might use it. He argues that being a 1:1 school tells parents only that there are enough laptops, not what their children are supposed to learn, and that leaders who spent years getting devices into schools now owe the same attention to what happens after students open them. He rejects both extremes, saying a wasteful tool should be dropped but removing every screen is not an instructional plan, and the decision must weigh the student, the task and the tool. His proposed approach is limits plus: clear boundaries paired with education in digital wellness, self-regulation and digital kindness, built on a Digital Driver's License model and a default-off classroom device. He closes with a practical sequence for leadership teams, from agreeing what a healthy school day looks like to inventorying applications and communicating proactively with families.
points: A school that answers a parent's question with 'we are a 1:1 school' has described its inventory, not its instructional purpose.
Technology decisions should look at the student, the task and the tool, so a wasteful tool gets dropped and a useful one gets a clear explanation.
Limits plus pairs firm boundaries, such as phone restrictions, with teaching students to self-regulate, respond to cruelty online and put a device down.
The Digital Driver's License borrows the driving model of instruction, supervised practice and demonstrated readiness before independence.
Leadership teams should agree on what a healthy school day looks like, then audit applications, set when devices stay closed and communicate openly with families.
quotes: If a parent asks why their child needs a laptop for a lesson, “we’re a 1:1 school” is a lousy answer. It tells them we have enough laptops. It doesn’t tell them what their child is supposed to learn.
We have been very good at getting devices into schools. We have not always given the same attention to what happens after students open them.
None of that makes removing every screen a sound instructional plan. If a tool is wasting students’ time, stop using it.

A phone restriction can protect instructional time. It does not, by itself, teach a student how to respond to a cruel group chat, recognize when an app is consuming too much of their attention, or put a device down without an adult directing them.
In the book, I describe this as limits plus: clear boundaries paired with education in digital wellness, self-regulation, and digital kindness.

A classroom device stays closed until there is a clear reason to use it. The teacher makes that decision based on the learning, and students learn that choosing when to use a tool is part of using it well.
If a tool remains in use mainly because the school has always paid for it, renewal season is a good time to ask a few uncomfortable questions.
We owe it to them to be intentional about the technology we put in their hands and honest about whether it is helping them learn.
